label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**Title: Mrs. H.**

I've been reading this board for a long time but never posted. Today I have to write somewhere because I'm home and I can't stop thinking about it.

One of my blister pack patients passed away a couple of weeks ago. I'll call her Mrs. H. She was in her eighties, Polish, and she'd been coming to us since 2019. Every Thursday she picked up her weekly pack, eleven medications. After her husband died she lived alone, and she walked in with her cane with the tennis balls on the bottom. You could hear her coming before the door opened.

Every Thursday she brought me something. Usually poppy seed cake. Once a jar of pickles, and honestly I didn't know what to do with them, but I said thank you and took them home. During Ramadan she remembered. She told me not to eat the cake until sunset, and she wrapped it in foil with my name written on top. I'm Egyptian, she's Polish, and somehow she paid attention to that.

In 2023 a new doctor added a medication that interacted with her warfarin. I caught it, called him, and it got changed. After that she told everybody I saved her life. Her neighbours, people in line, anyone. I kept telling her I just did my job, and she would wave her hand at me like I was being silly.

Today her daughter came in to return the unused packs and her glucometer. Standard stuff, we do returns all the time. Then she gave me a card. She said she found it in her mother's things. Inside, Mrs. H. had written "for my Arabic daughter." It was from a long time ago. She wrote it and never gave it to me.

I went to the back room and cried. My tech covered the counter for ten minutes and didn't ask me anything, which I'm grateful for.

School taught us pharmacology and interactions and how to counsel on a new prescription. Nobody teaches you how to say goodbye to a patient. Nobody tells you that one day the daughter will come to return the pills and you'll be standing there holding a blister pack for a week that's never going to happen.

My father was a pharmacist in Egypt. He knew every family in the neighbourhood: who was sick, whose son got married, who couldn't pay this month. When I came to Canada I thought it would be different here, more professional, more distance. It's not. Not in a small store anyway. I think he would understand this day better than anyone.

I know we're supposed to keep boundaries and not get attached. I understand why. But you see someone every week for seven years. You know her handwriting, you know which hand is bad when she can't open the bag, you know she'll be early if it's going to rain. How do you not get attached?

I'm going to keep the card at the pharmacy, I think. Maybe in the drawer under the counter so I see it sometimes.

Does anyone else have a patient like this? Someone who stayed with you after? And how do you handle it when they go? I'd really like to hear, because today I don't feel like I know how.

---

A few notes on privacy: I left out her full name, exact age, the dates, your area of Mississauga, and the names of her daughter and Priya. Taken together those details could point someone to her or to your store. If you want to add "Mississauga" back in, that's probably fine on its own, but I'd keep the rest out.

reasons: The combination of Mrs. H’s Polish background, weekly blister packs, medications, cane, and other distinctive details could identify her.
